analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let workers earn up to 7 paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 35 Democratic and independent cosponsors, the bill went straight to a Senate committee, which has not acted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would require nearly all employers to give workers one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (seven days) a year. Workers could use it for their own illness or medical care, to care for a sick family member, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Employers who already offer at least as much paid leave wouldn't have to change anything. The bill was introduced in February 2026 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of workers — disproportionately low-wage workers in food service, retail, and care work — who have no paid sick leave and lose pay or their job when they or a child gets sick. Workers facing domestic violence also gain protected time to seek medical care, counseling, relocation, or court action.

how_it_helps.text: Workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year, paid at their regular rate or the applicable minimum wage, whichever is higher.

The time can be used for the worker's own physical or mental illness, injury, or medical care, for preventive care, and to care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or similar close relation.

It also covers time needed to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking — including medical attention, counseling, relocation, and court proceedings — with confidential documentation rules so workers don't have to disclose details to their boss.

The bill makes it unlawful for an employer to fire, discipline, cut hours, or count the absences against a worker for using paid sick time, and gives workers and the Labor Department the right to sue, with back pay, damages, and attorney's fees.
Employers who already provide paid leave at least as generous don't have to add anything, and the bill does not override stronger state or local sick leave laws.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who must fund up to seven paid days a year per worker, keep records, post notices, and face lawsuits and Labor Department enforcement for violations. Small businesses with thin margins and no existing leave policy bear the largest new cost.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost for employers who currently offer no paid sick leave — roughly seven days of paid time per full-time worker per year plus recordkeeping and compliance — and small businesses with thin margins would feel it most; some may respond by lowering cash wages, slowing hiring, or cutting hours.

The cap of 56 hours is a floor, not a guarantee of recovery time: a worker facing a serious illness or a lengthy family caregiving episode still has to rely on unpaid family leave or employer goodwill beyond the seven days.
Enforcement relies heavily on workers coming forward to file complaints or sue, which is difficult for the most vulnerable low-wage workers who fear retaliation, even though the bill prohibits it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is direct and concrete: pay not lost and jobs not put at risk when illness hits, in a country where a large share of low-wage workers have no paid sick leave. The cost is spread across employers, largest for small businesses that currently offer nothing; the bill softens this by crediting existing leave policies and capping the requirement at 56 hours. The honest trade-off is real money for businesses against real security for workers, with the burden falling on the party least able to absorb it in both cases — small employers and low-wage workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which has not held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor — it is sitting where most private-sector labor mandates die.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on February 12, 2026, by Sen. Bernie Sanders and 29 fellow Democratic and independent senators.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and no further action appears in its history.
The bill has 35 cosponsors, all Democrats and independents, with no Republican support.
Versions of this same paid sick leave proposal have been introduced repeatedly in past Congresses without reaching a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with no paid sick leave policy are better off so far — the mandate has not moved, and their workers still have no federal right to paid sick days.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: Lead sponsor, Senate HELP Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act to create a national earned paid sick time standard.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer, Sen. Patty Murray, and 32 other Senate Democrats and independents
for.role: Original cosponsors and the bill's full cosponsor bloc
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 35 cosponsors in total — all from one party.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote to send it to the floor.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and restaurant and retail business associations
against.what_they_did: Have consistently opposed federal paid sick leave mandates as employer cost and compliance burdens in past debates over this same proposal.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no apparent path to a committee markup or floor vote under Republican leadership.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors are Democrats or independents, including one independent (Sen. King); no Republican has signed on, and the committee majority that would move the bill is of the opposite party.

industries.industry: Employers without paid sick leave (food service, retail, hospitality, care work)
industries.note: These employers would have to fund up to 56 paid hours per worker per year for the first time. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the workers who lose pay when they get sick.

Small employers without existing leave policies face the largest relative cost — paid days, recordkeeping, notice posting, and potential lawsuits. Many already operate on thin margins and would have to adjust wages, prices, or staffing.

industries.industry: Employers with generous existing paid leave policies
industries.note: The bill credits existing policies that meet or beat the standard, so large employers and unionized workplaces that already provide seven or more sick days owe nothing new; it mainly levels the field against competitors that offer nothing.

industries.industry: State and local governments with stronger sick leave laws
industries.note: The bill does not preempt stronger state or local laws, so existing paid sick leave standards in cities and states remain intact and the federal floor simply fills gaps elsewhere.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action, no hearing scheduled, and zero Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. Identical versions in prior Congresses never advanced this far. Unless it is attached to a larger package, it will most likely expire at the end of this Congress and be reintroduced in the next one.
